WALVIS BAY – The Walvis Bay municipality will not increase its tariffs for water and other related services for the current financial year.
This is despite outstanding debt by residents and institutions standing at N$293 million. The council did also not increase such tariffs during the previous financial year. This is according to the chairperson of the management committee Leroy Victor who tabled the 2021/2022 budget last week.
Victor said the council is expecting to generate N$759 million while their expenditure is equal to their expected revenue. “No tariff adjustments on these services are proposed for the two consecutive financial years, despite the fact that service providers such as NamWater might increase their tariffs later this year. However, the council has managed to balance its operational budget as required,” he said. He added residents should thus make use of the current amnesty meant to assist them in paying off their debt. “Amnesty interest will write off all outstanding interest levied once the capital amount has been settled in full and is in force until 31 December,” he said. Walvis Bay mayor Trevino Forbes earlier explained the initial debt in April this year stood at N$416 million with the council owing nothing to NamWater. “Considering the current outstanding service debt, I would humbly encourage our residents to keep on paying their utilities as this will provide the council with much needed revenue to execute its duties,” Forbes said. He earlier attributed the high debt to the downward economic trajectory, Covid-19, unauthorised water reconnections and leakages among others. “We still ensured that the council pays its bills to our service providers. I think it is only fair for the public to also grant council the same courtesy by ensuring that they pay or make the necessary arrangements to settle their accounts,” said Forbes.

a6832.t:
The former Chairman of Ghana’s Parliamentary Finance Committee and Member of Parliament for Okaikwei Central, Patrick Yaw Boamah has urged the nation to pivot from its reliance on imports and foreign aid toward a robust, self-sustaining industrial base.
In a statement copied to GraphicOnline, Mr Boamah underscored the urgent need to bolster local industries, particularly in pharmaceuticals, agro-processing, and textiles, to curb imports, boost exports, and fortify Ghana’s economy.
His remarks come at a critical juncture for Ghana, a nation grappling with economic vulnerabilities exacerbated by its dependence on foreign goods and support schemes like the African Growth and Opportunity Act (agoa).
 
While acknowledging the benefits of agoa, which grants preferential trade access to the United States for eligible African nations, the Okaikwei Central MP and former Chairman of the Finance Committee of Parliament cautioned against viewing it as a long-term crutch.
“An extension of agoa is welcome, but it cannot be indefinite,” he asserted. “We must wean ourselves from these policies and take deliberate steps to strengthen our own economic foundation.”
Central to Boamah’s vision is the development of competitive local industries capable of driving job creation and generating foreign exchange. He argued that Ghana’s economic aspirations—sustained growth, reduced unemployment, and global market relevance—hinge on the nation’s ability to produce rather than consume. “We cannot afford to sit back and be spoon-fed,” he said. “The time for strategic action is now.”
Reflecting on government initiatives, Boamah defended the One District, One Factory program, a flagship policy aimed at establishing industrial enterprises across Ghana’s districts. Despite criticisms and implementation challenges, he maintained that such efforts are vital to building local capacity. “Without bold steps to industrialize, the job creation we’ve been promising will remain an illusion,” he warned.
Boamah highlighted several sectors ripe for investment, emphasizing their potential to transform Ghana’s economic landscape. In pharmaceuticals, he pointed to local companies like Tobinco, Ernest Chemist, and Kinapharma as candidates for greater support to produce medicines domestically, reducing reliance on costly imports. The textile industry, he noted, holds untapped potential to generate significant revenue through exports, provided it receives adequate investment. Agro-processing also featured prominently in his remarks, with Mr Boamah urging the government to prioritize agribusiness as a cornerstone of economic diversification.
However, Mr Boamah was clear that rhetoric alone will not suffice. He called for substantial financial commitments to these sectors, arguing that meaningful progress requires more than promises. “If we want to compete in global markets with our crops and products, we must be prepared to invest heavily in their growth,” he said.
This, he stressed, demands not only funding but also strategic planning and unwavering political will.
He painted a vivid picture of a Ghana unshackled from dependency, poised to chart its own economic destiny.
“We cannot wait another twenty years, banking on agoa or external aid strategic thinking, real investment, and strong leadership are what will propel us forward," he stated.

a6890.t:
A constatação de que a maioria da população considera que a ajuda tem sido mal utilizada já serve de travão a eventuais acções do partido democrata em procurar contrariar o bloqueio da ajuda externa. E no mundo já se percebe que o impacto vai ser enorme, considerando que a contribuição americana de 40 bilhões de dólares anuais através da USAID corresponde a 40% da ajuda internacional.
De facto, é de esperar o efeito desastroso que a diminuição drástica dos fluxos da ajuda terá tanto directamente sobre muitos necessitados de alimento e medicamentos como indirectamente sobre as organizações de apoio que sem o suporte americano dificilmente vão poder prosseguir com a sua actividade humanitária. Uma outra consequência da medida é que poderá levar à imitação em outros países, designadamente na Europa, se os avanços da direita radical se traduzirem numa maioria que questiona a efectividade dos programas actuais de redução da pobreza, de ajuda humanitária e de apoio ao desenvolvimento e à luta contra as alterações climáticas. Sem doações substantivas dos dois maiores contribuidores, EUA e UE, muitos países e populações poderão ficar em situação difícil, particularmente em casos de catástrofes naturais, guerras e perseguições políticas, étnicas ou religiosas.
Não é fácil para qualquer país encontrar a fórmula certa para o crescimento económico e para o desenvolvimento. O baixo número de casos bem-sucedidos deveria ter servido de aviso. Aliás, a história da humanidade, que aponta para a revolução industrial, há trezentos atrás, como o momento quando se tornou possível o aumento da produtividade que levou ao crescimento e à criação sustentada de riqueza, deixa entender precisamente isso. Não obstante, insistiu-se na ideia que a ajuda externa podia substituir lideranças competentes, políticas próprias baseadas nas especificidades dos países e a vontade engajada das populações para se atingir o desenvolvimento. Sem desprimor pelos benefícios reais conseguidos com a generosidade internacional, permitiu-se que muito dos recursos disponibilizados tenham sido mal aproveitados, alimentando burocracias internacionais e nacionais e levando agora à percepção em várias franjas da população dos países doadores que afinal a ajuda não chega a quem mais precisa.
Para vários países em desenvolvimento a ajuda externa passou a representar algo similar ao chamado “resource curse”, ou maldição dos recursos, em que países com petróleo, diamante e outros minérios ricos são mal governados, têm instituições frágeis, apresentam grandes desigualdades sociais e não conseguem libertar-se da extrema pobreza. Segundo um paper do Banco Mundial “Aid and Resource Curse”, a ajuda externa também pode ser um factor para os governos não fazerem reformas, para serem despesistas, para optarem por projectos financiáveis e não pelos prioritários e para propiciarem rendas a clientelas políticas. Um outro efeito negativo referido no texto é o facto da administração dos projectos com os seus altos salários “subtrair” quadros qualificados ao Estado, enfraquecendo as instituições.
Quando o país em desenvolvimento se deixa apanhar por alguma forma do “aid curse”, é interessante notar como desenvolve narrativas, adopta atitudes e faz opções que racionalizam a sua permanência por largas décadas como recipiente da ajuda internacional. Alimenta, por exemplo, a narrativa que os recursos do país são objecto de cobiça dos estrangeiros e com isso justifica a desconfiança no investimento estrangeiro e no turismo. Nutre o ressentimento em direcção aos maiores doadores, ao mesmo tempo que incentiva uma cultura de vitimização histórica. Opta por políticas de distribuição de rendimento que não põem suficiente ênfase na necessidade de crescimento e criação de riqueza, mas privilegiam a formação de clientelas para a conquista e manutenção do poder.
O resultado é que não se consegue potenciar os fluxos de capital e os fluxos turísticos que teimam em chegar ao país, nem mobilizar a iniciativa, a criatividade e o espírito empresarial a quem se incutiu a ideia que há ganho em ser vítima e que a vantagem maior é ficar bem colocado na “cadeia alimentar” com o Estado no topo para ter acessos, favores e oportunidade de rendimento. Um outro resultado é que o país, apanhado num círculo vicioso, não consegue desenvolver uma ideia de desenvolvimento que podia contrapor às agendas das organizações de ajuda internacional, ficando sob uma espécie de tutela. Submetendo-se, o país aprofunda ainda mais a atitude do Estado rentista em que a política partidária deriva cada vez mais para soluções populistas que se alimentam do ressentimento social e incidem sobre a redistribuição de rendimentos, sem correspondência com a realidade presente e sem muita preocupação com o futuro.
Em Cabo Verde, nos últimos dias é interessante notar como os problemas do país são geralmente percebidos. A propósito do acordo de pesca com a União Europeia, a atenção geral fixou-se numa afirmação que Cabo Verde estaria a vender o atum por 13 escudos o quilo. É uma das tais afirmações que ressoam com narrativas bem estabelecidas segundo as quais o país é rico em peixe e, se não parece ser, é porque está sendo roubado. Devia ser evidente que Cabo Verde não vende peixe. Vende quem investe em navios e equipamentos e contrata pescadores para captura e depois leva o pescado ao mercado. No quadro do acordo com a UE cobra-se uma licença para explorar um recurso que na sua trajetória migratória passa pela sua zona económica exclusiva. Não há como confundir preço de venda de um produto pelo custo de uma licença de exploração de um recurso. Só se insiste nisso para reforçar a narrativa que alimenta fantasias e vitimiza a população, mas não leva a acção consequente.
De facto, se há um recurso como o peixe, porque não explorá-lo. Se se quer evitar que seja delapidado ilegalmente por outros, por que não fiscalizar a ZEE do país. Em quase cinquenta anos de independência, não se criou capacidade de captura industrial de peixe, nem se explorou acordos de pesca com países vizinhos: eles sim, são ricos em peixe. Também não se optou pela aposta numa guarda costeira para fiscalização das águas do país. Ou seja, não se agiu numa perspectiva de desenvolvimento do sector das pescas e a cooperação com vários países no sector ao longo de todos esses anos serviu outros propósitos que não os que deviam ser óbvios. Mesmo quando a UE facultou a possibilidade de exportação de peixe enlatado com isenção de tarifas, não foi compreendido que o país tinha um tempo para adquirir capacidade de captura para beneficiar das isenções. As derrogações à regra das normas de origem têm um prazo, findo o qual há consequências para as conserveiras, para os trabalhadores e para as exportações do país. Tudo parece não importar enquanto numa mistura de deleite e indignação se traz à colação a questão da extinção dos tubarões fundamentalmente para dar mais vitalidade à narrativa que o país tem recursos e estão a ser roubados.
Há, porém, que perceber que o mundo está a mudar e rapidamente. Os Estados Unidos congelaram a ajuda internacional e se não a retomarem, nem a UE poderá compensar o buraco. Se a tendência para a revisão da política de ajuda continuar, menos recursos serão disponibilizados para os países em desenvolvimento. Se os países que se deixaram imobilizar, apanhados pelo “aid curse”, não saírem do torpor, as consequências poderão ser terríveis. Em Cabo Verde, com o mundo a transformar-se radicalmente não se pode ficar por mais tempo a deixar-se embalar por narrativas fantasiosas que impedem o desenvolvimento, vitimizam as populações e desresponsabilizam as instituições.
Humberto Cardoso
Texto originalmente publicado na edição impressa do Expresso das Ilhas nº 1212 de 19 de Fevereiro de 2025.
a6890.en:
The finding that the majority of the population considers that aid has been badly used already serves as a brake on any possible actions by the Democratic party to try to counter the blocking of foreign aid. And around the world it is already understood that the impact will be enormous, considering that the American contribution of 40 billion dollars a year through USAID corresponds to 40% of international aid.

Indeed, one can expect the disastrous effect that the drastic reduction in aid flows will have both directly on many people in need of food and medicines and indirectly on the support organisations which, without American backing, will hardly be able to continue their humanitarian activity. Another consequence of the measure is that it may lead to imitation in other countries, notably in Europe, if the advances of the radical right translate into a majority that questions the effectiveness of current programmes of poverty reduction, humanitarian aid, and support for development and the fight against climate change. Without substantive donations from the two largest contributors, the US and the EU, many countries and populations could find themselves in a difficult situation, particularly in cases of natural disasters, wars and political, ethnic or religious persecution.

It is not easy for any country to find the right formula for economic growth and development. The low number of successful cases should have served as a warning. Indeed, the history of humanity, which points to the industrial revolution three hundred years ago as the moment when it became possible to increase productivity in a way that led to growth and the sustained creation of wealth, suggests precisely that. Nevertheless, people insisted on the idea that foreign aid could substitute for competent leadership, for policies of one's own based on the specificities of countries, and for the engaged will of populations in achieving development. Without denying the real benefits achieved through international generosity, it was allowed that much of the resources made available were badly used, feeding international and national bureaucracies and now leading to the perception among various segments of the populations of donor countries that after all the aid does not reach those who need it most.

For several developing countries, foreign aid has come to represent something similar to the so-called “resource curse”, in which countries with oil, diamonds and other rich minerals are badly governed, have fragile institutions, present large social inequalities and cannot free themselves from extreme poverty. According to a World Bank paper, “Aid and Resource Curse”, foreign aid can also be a factor in governments not carrying out reforms, in being spendthrift, in opting for financeable rather than priority projects, and in providing rents to political clienteles. Another negative effect mentioned in the text is the fact that the administration of projects, with its high salaries, “subtracts” qualified personnel from the State, weakening institutions.

When a developing country lets itself be caught by some form of the “aid curse”, it is interesting to note how it develops narratives, adopts attitudes and makes choices that rationalise its remaining for long decades as a recipient of international aid. It feeds, for example, the narrative that the country's resources are the object of foreigners' covetousness and with that justifies distrust of foreign investment and tourism. It nurtures resentment towards the largest donors, while at the same time encouraging a culture of historical victimisation. It opts for income distribution policies that do not place sufficient emphasis on the need for growth and wealth creation, but instead privilege the formation of clienteles for the conquest and maintenance of power.

The result is that the country fails to make the most of the capital flows and tourist flows that persist in arriving, nor to mobilise the initiative, creativity and entrepreneurial spirit of those who have been instilled with the idea that there is gain in being a victim and that the greatest advantage is to be well positioned in the “food chain” with the State at the top, in order to have access, favours and income opportunities. Another result is that the country, caught in a vicious circle, cannot develop an idea of development that it could set against the agendas of international aid organisations, remaining under a kind of tutelage. By submitting, the country deepens still further the attitude of the rentier State, in which party politics drifts more and more towards populist solutions that feed on social resentment and focus on income redistribution, without correspondence to present reality and without much concern for the future.

In Cabo Verde, in recent days it is interesting to note how the country's problems are generally perceived. Regarding the fisheries agreement with the European Union, general attention has fixed on a claim that Cabo Verde was selling tuna at 13 escudos a kilo. It is one of those claims that resonate with well-established narratives according to which the country is rich in fish and, if it does not appear to be, that is because it is being robbed. It should be obvious that Cabo Verde does not sell fish. Those who sell are those who invest in vessels and equipment and hire fishermen for the catch and then take the fish to market. Under the framework of the agreement with the EU, a licence is charged for exploiting a resource which, on its migratory path, passes through the country's exclusive economic zone. There is no way to confuse the sale price of a product with the cost of a licence to exploit a resource. People only insist on this to reinforce the narrative that feeds fantasies and victimises the population, but it leads to no consequential action.

In fact, if there is a resource such as fish, why not exploit it. If one wants to prevent it from being illegally plundered by others, why not police the country's EEZ. In almost fifty years of independence, no capacity for industrial fish catching has been created, nor have fisheries agreements with neighbouring countries been explored: they indeed are rich in fish. Nor was there a choice to invest in a coastguard to police the country's waters. That is to say, there was no action from the perspective of developing the fisheries sector, and the cooperation with various countries in the sector over all these years served other purposes than those which should have been obvious. Even when the EU granted the possibility of exporting canned fish free of tariffs, it was not understood that the country had a window of time to acquire catching capacity in order to benefit from the exemptions. Derogations from the rules of origin have a deadline, after which there are consequences for the canneries, for the workers and for the country's exports. None of it seems to matter while, in a mixture of delight and indignation, the question of the extinction of sharks is brought up essentially to give more vitality to the narrative that the country has resources and they are being stolen.

One must, however, realise that the world is changing, and fast. The United States has frozen international aid and if it does not resume it, not even the EU will be able to compensate for the hole. If the trend towards revising aid policy continues, fewer resources will be made available to developing countries. If the countries that let themselves be immobilised, caught by the “aid curse”, do not emerge from their torpor, the consequences could be terrible. In Cabo Verde, with the world transforming radically, one can no longer go on letting oneself be lulled by fanciful narratives that impede development, victimise populations and absolve institutions of responsibility.

Humberto Cardoso

Text originally published in the print edition of Expresso das Ilhas no. 1212 of 19 February 2025.

Muktasari:
- Tanzania, India na Marekani zimeungana kwa pamoja ili kuchochea juhudi za matumizi ya nishati safi na nishati jadidifu kwa kuwajengea uwezo wataalamu wa nchi hizo.
Dar es Salaam. Tanzania imeanza kuwanoa wataalamu wake wa nishati ikiwa ni hatua ya kwanza kuelekea uzalishaji wa megawati zaidi ya 1,000 zitokanazo na nishati jadidifu mwaka 2045, kwa ajili ya gridi ya Taifa.
Ili kufanikisha hilo, India, Marekani na Tanzania zimefikia makubaliano ya ushirikiano kwa ajili ya kubadilishana uzoefu na kuwapatia mafunzo wataalamu wa pande zote ili kuchochea matumizi ya nishati safi na nishati jadidifu.
Kufanya hivi kunalenga kupunguza athari za matumizi ya nishati nyingine kama kuni na mkaa kupikia, huku kuongeza uzalishaji wa umeme kupitia vyanzo vingine ukilenga kupunguza ukosekanaji wa umeme katika baadhi ya maeneo nchini.
Hayo yameelezwa leo Julai 17,2024 katika hafla ya uzinduzi wa ushirikiano wa nchi hizo tatu, Kamishna Msaidizi wa Nishati jadidifu kutoka Wizara ya Nishati, Imani Mruma.
Mruma amesema mpaka sasa ni megawati 10.5 pekee za umeme utokanao na nishati jadidifu unaoingia katika gridi ya Taifa hivyo malengo ni kuziongeza.
Amesema kwa sasa ipo miradi mbalimbali inayotekelezwa ukiwamo wa Kishapu mkoani Shinyanga wa umeme jua utakaokuwa na uwezo wa kuzalisha megawati 15, mradi wa joto ardhi mkoani Songwe utakaozalisha megawati 200.
Amesema miradi mingine iko katika upembuzi yakinifu ikijumuisha ya upepo katika mikoa ya Iringa, Njombe, Singida, Shinyanga na Kilimanjaro.
“Tunategemea miradi hii kwa ujumla hadi mwaka 2028 itakuja kutuzalishia megawati 843 tuko hatua nzuri na lengo letu hadi mwaka 2045 tuingize zaidi ya megawati 1,000 katika gridi ya Taifa kupitia mpango wa kitaifa wa kuendeleza nishati nchini,” amesema Mruma.
Akizungumzia ushirikiano huo, Naibu Katibu Mkuu wa Wizara ya Nishati, Dk James Mataragio amesema Marekani na India wamepiga hatua katika suala la matumizi ya nishati safi na jadidifu, huku Tanzania ikiianza safari hiyo.
“Kuna kampeni kubwa sasa hivi hapa Tanzania ya matumizi ya nishati safi ya kupikia, kama nchi tunajaribu kusukuma utekelezaji wa kampeni hiyo ndiyo maana tunajiunga na wenzetu wa Marekani na India ambao wana uzoefu katika eneo hili ili kufua vijana wetu ,” amesema Mataragio.
Balozi Mdogo wa Ubalozi wa India Tanzania, Manoj Verma amesema wana uhakika ushirikiano huo wa maendeleo kati ya nchi tatu utawawezesha wengine kutumia uzoefu wa India katika eneo la nishati mbadala, kuboresha maisha ya Watanzania kwa njia endelevu.
Kaimu Mkurugenzi Mkazi wa USAID nchini, Alexander Klaits amesema ushirikiano huo utaimarisha uwezo wa ndani na kuongeza fursa za biashara baina ya kampuni za Marekani nchini Tanzania.
a7021.en:
Summary:
- Tanzania, India and the United States have joined together to spur efforts on the use of clean energy and renewable energy by building the capacity of experts from those countries.

Dar es Salaam. Tanzania has begun sharpening the skills of its energy experts as a first step towards producing more than 1,000 megawatts from renewable energy by 2045 for the national grid.

To achieve this, India, the United States and Tanzania have reached a cooperation agreement to exchange experience and to provide training to experts from all sides in order to spur the use of clean energy and renewable energy.

Doing this aims to reduce the effects of the use of other fuels such as firewood and charcoal for cooking, while increasing electricity generation through other sources, with the aim of reducing the lack of electricity in some areas of the country.

This was explained today, 17 July 2024, at the launch ceremony of the cooperation between these three countries, by the Assistant Commissioner for Renewable Energy from the Ministry of Energy, Imani Mruma.

Mruma said that so far only 10.5 megawatts of electricity from renewable energy enters the national grid, so the goal is to increase it.

He said that at present there are various projects being implemented, including the Kishapu solar project in Shinyanga region, which will have the capacity to generate 15 megawatts, and a geothermal project in Songwe region which will produce 200 megawatts.

He said other projects are at the feasibility study stage, including wind projects in the regions of Iringa, Njombe, Singida, Shinyanga and Kilimanjaro.

“We expect these projects altogether to produce 843 megawatts for us by 2028. We are at a good stage, and our goal by 2045 is to bring more than 1,000 megawatts into the national grid through the national plan for developing energy in the country,” said Mruma.

Speaking about this cooperation, the Deputy Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Energy, Dr James Mataragio, said the United States and India have made strides on the matter of using clean and renewable energy, while Tanzania is beginning that journey.

“There is a big campaign right now here in Tanzania on the use of clean cooking energy; as a country we are trying to push the implementation of that campaign, and that is why we are joining our colleagues from the United States and India, who have experience in this area, in order to train our young people,” said Mataragio.

The Deputy High Commissioner of the Indian High Commission in Tanzania, Manoj Verma, said they are confident that this development cooperation between the three countries will enable others to use India’s experience in the area of alternative energy, improving the lives of Tanzanians in a sustainable way.

The Acting Resident Director of USAID in the country, Alexander Klaits, said the cooperation will strengthen local capacity and increase business opportunities between American companies in Tanzania.

a7057.t:
Floods and highway insecurities across South Sudan in September 2024 worsened humanitarian access as 15 major supply routes were rendered impassable, impacting the delivery of essential humanitarian supplies to some 500,000 people, according to an agency.
UN Office for Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said there were over 30 humanitarian access impediments last month, undermining the floods response and forcing relief organizations to resort to more costly air and river transport.
“Key access challenges included physical access constraints, violence against humanitarian personnel and assets, bureaucratic impediments and operational interference,” it said.
More than 890,000 people have been affected by flooding in 40 counties across South Sudan leading to massive displacement, loss of livelihoods and destruction of critical infrastructures, according to the UN humanitarian agency.
It further underscored that security situation along the Juba-Nimule Road, following an attack on a passenger bus, has posed a significant threat to the supply of essential goods to markets in Juba.
It stated that the abduction of humanitarian staff for ransom in Yei River County prompted MSF to suspend health services, leaving the population with reduced access to health care.
OCHA said other incidents that impeded access along major roads include ambushes, robberies, harassment and theft reported in the Equatoria region and the Abyei Administrative Area.
The UN agency points to bureaucratic impediments including multiple checkpoints along the Nile and the Sobat river, which it believes, continue to impact access to humanitarian assistance.
It also cites harassment of transport operators, interference with recruitment processes, boat seizures and the denial of access to quarrying sites in Malakal as factors delaying or increasing the cost of critical services.
